newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Diana sets to work in Angola for landmine campaign.
newsitem.headline: Diana sets to work in Angola for landmine campaign.

text.p: Britain's Princess Diana sped past the hovels of Angola's poorest on Monday as she arrived to lend her unrivalled publicity power to a Red Cross campaign to ban landmines worldwide.

Dropping her usual entourage for a lone butler, and dressed in practical jeans, navy jacket and sneakers, she made clear this was a working visit to a country where nine million landmines, one per person, still lie in wait for victims.
"There couldn't be a more appropriate place to begin a campaign than Angola," said Diana, whose public image could recover from last year's divorce doldrums by a stint of solid charity work.

"It is my sincere hope that by working together in the next few days we shall focus world attention on this vital, but until now largely neglected, issue. so let's go on," she told reporters in the capital, Luanda.

The British Red Cross hopes the hordes of journalists who follow Diana's every move -- even across the world to Angola -- will help focus attention on the campaign to outlaw landmines which kill or maim 2,000 people a month round the world.
The southern African state has three amputees per thousand people, the world's highest rate. Some 24 new victims are admitted to hospital each day.
Many are innocent civilians who stumbled onto mines still hidden despite the end of two decades of civil war in 1994.

The Princess of Wales -- a title she retains despite her bitter 1996 divorce from Britain's heir to the throne Prince Charles -- will meet mine victims, a common sight as they hobble on crutches on the streets of Luanda, during her four-day visit.
She will visit a Red Cross factory making artificial limbs, health centres and hospitals caring for war victims.
Red Cross officials, who briefed her in private on Monday, told Reuters that Diana, 35, had been particularly keen to know about the psychological support given to landmine victims.
Her usual staff, including a personal hairdresser, a dresser and a lady-in-waiting, stayed at home in icy Britain this time as Diana and one manservant headed for the tropical heat.

Her route after a low-key arrival took her through some of the capital's poorest areas, past seas of tin shanties where most people live without water and electricity, to the swish British ambassador's residence in town where she will stay.
Diana resigned as vice president of the British Red Cross after her July divorce, but by visiting Angola has shown she intends to keep up charity work she says means so much to her.
She has taken her two sons, William and Harry, to see London's own homeless and has been praised for her work with people suffering from AIDS when it was unfashionable.

Mike Whitlam, head of the British Red Cross, told reporters Diana's support did not mean she had returned to the Red Cross. "The world wants to know what she is doing and why she is doing it. And if that interest can be converted into interest on the landmines issue then we are pleased," he said.

British royal watchers say there has been a rethink about Diana's opting-out of charity work after the divorce, and if the Angola trip goes well, it could be followed by visits to trouble spots such as Bosnia and Afghanistan.
